body:
Changing artistic preferences

Mughal painting continued to develop under Akbar's successors. The most useful distinction is between Akbar's emphasis on extensive illustrated manuscript projects and Jahangir's strong interest in carefully observed individual paintings.

Jahangir: portraiture and the natural world

During the reign of Jahangir (1605–1627), painting reached a high level of refinement in portraiture and the depiction of animals, birds and plants.

Jahangir was an attentive observer of the natural world. Artists were encouraged to represent the distinctive appearance of individual creatures and people. This gave particular importance to detailed and realistic images.

Instead of relying primarily on large narrative manuscripts, Jahangir increasingly favoured individual paintings that could be gathered into albums, also called muraqqas.

Ustad Mansur

Ustad Mansur was a celebrated painter of birds and animals at Jahangir's court. His work is associated with unusually careful observation and detailed natural studies. Jahangir honoured him with the title Nadir ul Asr, meaning Wonder of the Age.

Well-known subjects associated with Mansur include a falcon and a zebra. These paintings are valuable examples of the emperor's interest in recording rare or remarkable creatures.

Abu'l Hasan

Abu'l Hasan was another prominent artist under Jahangir. He received the title Nadir al Zaman, meaning Wonder of the Time.

His painting commonly known as Jahangir's Dream depicts Jahangir embracing the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas. The scene was symbolic rather than a record of an actual meeting. It communicated a political image of the Mughal emperor's superiority.

Bishandas and Bichitra

Bishandas was admired for portraiture, including accurate representations of individuals. Bichitra is associated with elaborate symbolic compositions, including Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings, also known through its hourglass imagery.

European influence on Mughal pictures

Contacts with European visitors and the circulation of European pictures introduced additional artistic devices. These included new approaches to shading, modelling, perspective and Christian imagery.

Artists used these elements selectively. Mughal paintings remained products of the imperial workshop, with subjects and meanings shaped by their Indian and Persian cultural settings.

Shah Jahan: courtly splendour and formal portraits

Under Shah Jahan (1628–1658), painting continued to receive patronage. Many pictures emphasised imperial majesty, formal court appearances, costly clothing, jewellery and carefully arranged compositions.

The illustrated Badshahnama, also written as Padshahnama, is a major example. Its images represent court ceremonies and important events of Shah Jahan's reign.

Paintings from this period often show more formal poses and carefully ordered court scenes. These preferences differed from Jahangir's particular enthusiasm for intimate portraits and close studies of nature, although these artistic interests overlapped.

Later Mughal painting

As political power became more dispersed, many painters sought patronage outside the imperial court. Regional courts continued to commission paintings and adapted elements of the Mughal style to their own subjects and traditions.

This was a gradual process, not an immediate disappearance of Mughal painting. Artistic production continued in the imperial and regional traditions after the 17th century.

Prelims focus

  • Jahangir: renowned for individual portraits, albums and natural studies.
  • Ustad Mansur: celebrated painter of birds and animals.
  • Abu'l Hasan: associated with Jahangir's Dream.
  • Bishandas: recognised for portraiture.
  • Shah Jahan: associated with formal courtly images and the illustrated Badshahnama.
  • Trap: Jahangir's Dream was an allegorical painting, not evidence that Jahangir and Shah Abbas physically met.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Chapter 3, The Mughal School of Miniature Painting, sections on Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Later Mughal Painting, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 19 November 2026; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 9, Kings and Chronicles, printed pp. 229–232 and 249–250.]

pictures.alt: Akbar favoured narrative manuscripts, Jahangir portraits and nature, and Shah Jahan formal court images; themes overlapped across reigns.
pictures.caption: Imperial patrons encouraged different artistic emphases.

title: Mughal Painting under Jahangir and Shah Jahan

body:
Imperial and regional painting traditions

Mughal miniature painting developed alongside several regional traditions. These schools influenced one another, but their subjects, artistic conventions and patrons were not identical.

The movement of artists, manuscripts, paintings and patrons helped spread techniques between regions. The resulting works often combined local preferences with influences from the imperial workshop.

Important regional traditions

SchoolImportant centresCommon features and subjects
MughalAgra, Delhi and other imperial centresHistorical scenes, portraits, court ceremonies, animals and plants; careful detail and naturalism.
RajasthaniMewar, Marwar, Bundi, Bikaner, Jaipur and KishangarhRoyal life, religious narratives, Ragamala and poetic themes; varied local styles and strong colour.
PahariBasohli, Guler, Kangra and other western Himalayan courtsReligious and poetic subjects, especially Krishna themes; styles ranging from bold colour to delicate landscapes.
DeccaniBijapur, Golconda and other Deccan courtsRegional court subjects, imaginative compositions, rich colours and distinctive figure types.

Rajasthani painting

The Rajasthani schools flourished under regional rulers. They included several local traditions rather than one completely uniform style.

Mewar painting is associated with bold compositions and religious and literary subjects. Bundi developed distinctive treatments of landscapes, courtly life and poetic themes. Kishangarh later became especially associated with refined images of Krishna and Radha.

Mughal influences appeared in portraiture and court representation, but indigenous themes and painting conventions remained important.

Pahari painting

Pahari means hilly or mountainous. The Pahari schools developed in the western Himalayan region, particularly from the 17th century onward.

Basohli is known for vigorous lines and strong colours. The later Guler and Kangra developments showed greater delicacy, naturalistic landscape treatment and lyrical themes.

Many Pahari paintings illustrated episodes from the Ramayana, Bhagavata Purana and Krishna-related poetry. The mature Kangra style is especially associated with the later 18th century, so it should not be assigned to Akbar's imperial workshop.

Deccani painting

Painting also flourished at Deccan courts such as Bijapur and Golconda. Deccani artists drew upon local, Persian and other artistic influences. Their paintings often differed from Mughal works through imaginative settings, intense colours and distinctive compositions.

The Deccani schools developed under regional dynasties and should not be treated simply as branches established by Mughal emperors.

How artistic influences spread

Imperial and regional traditions interacted through gifts, marriages, court appointments and the movement of artists. When imperial patronage weakened, some artists found employment in regional courts and contributed to further exchanges of style.

Prelims focus

  • Mughal painting: imperial history, portraiture and naturalistic studies.
  • Rajasthani schools: Mewar, Bundi, Marwar, Bikaner, Jaipur and Kishangarh.
  • Pahari schools: Basohli, Guler and Kangra.
  • Deccani schools: associated with regional courts including Bijapur and Golconda.
  • Kangra painting developed especially under later regional patronage.
  • Trap: Mughal, Rajasthani, Pahari and Deccani are related but distinct painting traditions.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Chapter 2, The Rajasthani Schools of Painting; Chapter 3, The Mughal School of Miniature Painting; and Chapter 5, The Pahari Schools of Painting, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 19 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, section Painting for Patrons: The Tradition of Miniatures.]

pictures.alt: Persian, Indian and selected European influences enter Mughal painting; techniques spread to distinct regional courts, while artists move as patronage changes.
pictures.caption: Regional schools adapted influences rather than copying one another.

title: Regional Schools of Painting and Mughal Artistic Influence

body:
The development of Mughal architecture

Mughal architecture combined building traditions associated with Central Asia and Persia with materials, construction techniques and decorative practices already established in India.

Important Mughal buildings included forts, palaces, mosques, tombs, audience halls and gardens. The ruler, royal family and nobility provided significant patronage, while Indian craftsmen and specialist workers carried out construction.

Trabeate and arcuate construction

Two architectural principles help explain the structural forms found in medieval Indian buildings.

  • Trabeate construction: A horizontal beam or lintel rests on vertical pillars or supports. The weight above is carried by the beam and transferred to its supports.
  • Arcuate construction: A properly constructed arch transfers the weight above it through wedge-shaped masonry blocks acting in compression towards the supporting walls or piers.

Arches and domes became important in Indo-Islamic buildings. However, trabeate and arcuate methods could exist together in the same monument. Mughal architecture did not completely abandon pillars and lintels.

Important architectural terms

  • Chhatri: A small domed pavilion, commonly supported by pillars.
  • Jali: A perforated stone screen that allows light and air to pass through while creating decorative patterns.
  • Pishtaq: A monumental arched entrance or portal projecting prominently from a building's façade.
  • Pietra dura: Decorative inlay using carefully cut pieces of coloured stone set into a stone surface.
  • Arabesque: Ornament using flowing plant-like or interlacing patterns.
  • Calligraphy: Decorative writing used in inscriptions and architectural ornament.

Red sandstone and white marble became prominent materials. Carved floral motifs, geometric patterns, jalis, decorative inscriptions and stone inlay were used according to the building's purpose and the patron's preferences.

Charbagh: the formal Mughal garden

A charbagh, also written chahar bagh, is a garden divided into 4 principal sections, commonly by intersecting paths or water channels. The name means 4 gardens.

Water channels, pools, fountains and carefully arranged planting formed important features of Mughal garden design. Such gardens expressed ideas of order, beauty and the association between water and paradise.

Babur showed a strong interest in gardens. Later rulers developed formal garden design in royal residences, pleasure gardens and tomb complexes.

Central garden tomb and riverfront arrangement

In the formal arrangement of Humayun's Tomb, the mausoleum occupies a central position within a garden scheme.

The Taj Mahal presents a significant variation. Its white marble mausoleum stands at the northern, river-facing end of the garden rather than at the central crossing of the main garden paths.

Regional adaptation and Gujarat

Mughal architecture did not develop in isolation from earlier provincial traditions. Gujarat's Indo-Islamic architecture already combined features such as carved brackets, local ornamental motifs and forms associated with regional temple construction.

The Sarkhej complex near Ahmedabad, associated with Shaikh Ahmad Khattu and developed before Mughal rule in Gujarat, is an important example of the regional architectural tradition. Such provincial forms influenced later architectural development.

This is a distinction of chronology and patronage: an architectural feature that influenced Mughal building does not automatically make the earlier structure a Mughal monument.

Prelims focus

  • Trabeate: beam-and-support construction; arcuate: arch-based construction.
  • Jali: perforated stone screen; chhatri: small domed pavilion.
  • Pietra dura: coloured-stone inlay.
  • Charbagh: garden divided into 4 principal sections.
  • Humayun's Tomb uses a central garden-tomb arrangement.
  • Trap: The Taj Mahal's mausoleum stands towards the riverfront end of its garden, not at the centre of its charbagh.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 8, Some Aspects of Indo-Islamic Architecture, printed pp. 109–115 and 119–121; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, sections on Mughal gardens and tombs; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Humayun's Tomb, Delhi, and Taj Mahal, Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Water and planned planting were central to Mughal gardens.

title: Mughal Architecture: Building Techniques, Decoration and Gardens

body:
Identifying monuments by their historical associations

Major Mughal monuments can be distinguished through their patron, location, building material, function and characteristic architectural features. A tomb, palace, fort and mosque served different purposes, even when they shared the same decorative vocabulary.

Important monuments

MonumentLocationPatron or associationIdentifying fact
Humayun's TombDelhiCommissioned under the patronage of Humayun's family during Akbar's reign.Completed around 1570; landmark Mughal garden tomb.
Agra FortAgraMajor construction under Akbar; additions under Shah Jahan.Red sandstone imperial fort with later marble structures.
Fatehpur SikriNear AgraAkbarPlanned imperial city begun in 1571, with palaces, audience halls and Jama Masjid.
Akbar's TombSikandra, AgraBegun under Akbar and completed under Jahangir.Imperial mausoleum associated with Akbar.
Itimad-ud-Daulah's TombAgraNur JahanWhite marble mausoleum built for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, during 1622–1628.
Taj MahalAgraShah JahanWhite marble mausoleum built in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.
Red FortDelhiShah JahanPalace fort of Shahjahanabad with red sandstone walls and refined interiors.
Jama MasjidDelhiShah JahanMajor congregational mosque of Shahjahanabad.

Humayun's Tomb and the development of garden tombs

Humayun's Tomb is an important early landmark in Mughal imperial architecture. Completed in 1570, it combined a monumental tomb structure with an extensive formal garden. Its use of red sandstone, marble and carefully ordered geometry influenced later Mughal monuments.

Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar's planned imperial city

Akbar established Fatehpur Sikri as an imperial capital during the 1570s. Major construction began in 1571. The complex included administrative buildings, residences, religious structures and spaces for court ceremonies.

Notable buildings include the Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Am, Diwan-i-Khas, Jama Masjid and the tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti.

The Buland Darwaza, or Lofty Gate, commemorates Akbar's victory in Gujarat in 1572. UNESCO records its completion in 1575. It provides a direct connection between a major Mughal monument and the history of Gujarat.

The imperial capital was moved to Lahore in 1585. Fatehpur Sikri continued to be visited, but it did not remain the permanent Mughal capital.

The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah

Nur Jahan commissioned this tomb for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, who held the title Itimad-ud-Daulah. Built during 1622–1628, the monument is particularly associated with white marble, finely carved jalis and elaborate coloured-stone inlay.

It is sometimes called the Baby Taj, but it is a separate monument with a different patron and purpose.

The Taj Mahal and Shah Jahan's architecture

Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal in Agra in memory of Mumtaz Mahal. Construction began in the early 1630s. UNESCO records completion of the principal mausoleum by 1648 and the wider complex by 1653.

The monument is recognised through its white marble appearance, large central dome, 4 corner minarets, symmetrical arrangement, carved jalis, calligraphy and pietra dura ornament.

The principal mausoleum stands at the riverfront end of its formal garden, beside the Yamuna.

Shahjahanabad and the Red Fort

Shah Jahan developed the new capital of Shahjahanabad in Delhi. Its Red Fort was designed as an imperial palace fort.

The fort is distinguished by massive red sandstone outer walls and an interior containing royal pavilions. A water channel known as Nahr-i-Bihisht, or Stream of Paradise, connected important palace spaces.

Delhi's Jama Masjid was another major architectural project of Shah Jahan. It should not be confused with the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri, which belongs to Akbar's planned city.

Prelims focus

  • Humayun's Tomb: Delhi, completed around 1570.
  • Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar; Buland Darwaza commemorates the Gujarat victory.
  • Itimad-ud-Daulah's Tomb: commissioned by Nur Jahan for her father.
  • Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan, Mumtaz Mahal, Agra.
  • Red Fort of Shahjahanabad: Shah Jahan, Delhi.
  • Trap: Agra Fort and Delhi's Red Fort are different monuments; both have important Mughal associations.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 8, Some Aspects of Indo-Islamic Architecture, printed pp. 113–121; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Humayun's Tomb, Delhi; Fatehpur Sikri; Taj Mahal; and Red Fort Complex, Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 19 November 2026; Government of Uttar Pradesh, Agra District, Tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah, monument description, consulted 19 November 2026.]
